summary: Lists architectural and functional requirements for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance in the MPLS Transport Profile. They apply to pseudowires, label switched paths and sections. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5860 lists what Operations, Administration, and Maintenance tools for MPLS Transport Profile need to do. It covers path checks, fault reports, and performance measurements, while leaving the protocols that provide these functions to other documents.

questions: what are oam requirements for mpls transport
what is fate sharing in oam
subtitle: Architectural and functional requirements for monitoring and troubleshooting MPLS Transport Profile paths.

tldr.problem: MPLS Transport Profile operators need to detect, locate, and report faults and measure service performance across pseudowires, LSPs, and Sections.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets architectural requirements for OAM and lists functions including continuity checks, connectivity verification, route tracing, alarms, lock state, and packet loss and delay measurement.
tldr.outcome: It gives protocol designers a common requirements set but does not define or select the protocols that meet it. OAM packets must follow the same path as user traffic and must not cause congestion.

facts.label: OAM packet path
facts.value: In-band, same path as user traffic

facts.label: Packet loss ratio
facts.value: User packets lost / user packets sent during an interval

today: RFC 5860 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2010. It specifies requirements, while the protocols that meet them are defined elsewhere; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What MPLS-TP OAM Is For
sections.content:
Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) supports both network operation and customer-service monitoring in the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP). Network operators use it to monitor infrastructure and support actions such as protection after a node or link failure. Service providers use it to monitor customer services and check Service Level Agreement parameters.

OAM can reduce operating complexity, improve network availability by finding faults before customers report them, and help identify service degradation such as packet delay or loss. The requirements in this RFC apply to pseudowires, Label Switched Paths (LSPs), and Sections. It lists requirements only; protocol solutions and guidance about which function to use for a particular application are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS-TP OAM gives operators ways to check paths, find faults, and measure service performance. This RFC states what those tools need to support, not how they are implemented.

sections.title: Architectural Requirements
sections.content:
OAM solutions MUST apply at least to point-to-point bidirectional pseudowires, co-routed bidirectional LSPs, and bidirectional Sections. They must work end-to-end and on segments, across domains, and at any label-stack depth. Solutions SHOULD be independent of the underlying transmission technology and of the service emulated by a pseudowire.

OAM packets MUST run in-band and follow the same data path as user traffic for the relevant pseudowire, LSP, or Section. This is called fate sharing. Implementations MUST be able to distinguish OAM packets from user traffic and apply specific treatment to OAM packets.

OAM MUST work with or without IP capabilities and MUST be configurable without a control plane. When OAM is enabled or disabled after a connection is established, the customer MUST NOT perceive service degradation. Where MPLS-TP runs with IP routing and forwarding, existing OAM protocols such as LSP-Ping, MPLS-BFD, VCCV, and VCCV-BFD must remain usable.
sections.plainLanguage: OAM messages must travel along the same path as the traffic they check. The system must also support operation without IP capabilities or a control plane.

sections.title: Checking Continuity, Connectivity, and Routes
sections.content:
The OAM toolset MUST detect, diagnose, and locate faults or defects on pseudowires, LSPs, and Sections, and notify appropriate nodes. A service provider MUST be able to learn about a fault affecting its service even when the fault lies outside its domain.

Continuity checks let an End Point monitor whether a path is live and SHOULD be proactive. Connectivity verification lets an End Point check that it is connected to the expected endpoint over the expected path; it SHOULD run proactively between End Points and on demand for other checks. Route tracing discovers the End Points and Intermediate Points along a path, including node and interface identifiers, and SHOULD be on demand.

Diagnostic tests MUST be available. Examples include looping OAM and data traffic back to the originating End Point and estimating an LSP's bandwidth. These tests SHOULD be on demand.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators need to check whether a path is live, whether it reaches the expected endpoint, and which nodes it crosses. They also need on-demand tests for troubleshooting.

sections.title: Lock, Alarm, and Defect Reports
sections.content:
An End Point MUST be able to instruct its peer End Points to lock a pseudowire, LSP, or Section. A lock is an administrative state in which only test traffic, if any, and OAM for that path are expected. Lock instruct SHOULD be on demand.

Intermediate Points MUST be able to report a lock on a tunnel LSP when it indirectly affects a pseudowire or LSP, and MUST be able to report a tunnel fault or defect that indirectly affects it. These lock and alarm reports SHOULD be proactive. An End Point MUST also be able to report a fault or defect it detects to its associated End Point.

Client Failure Indication MUST carry a client-layer fault or defect from one edge to the other when the client layer does not provide its own alarm propagation. These remote and client failure indications SHOULD be proactive.
sections.plainLanguage: OAM must carry information about local and underlying-path failures to the endpoints that need it. It must also support locking a path for maintenance or testing.

sections.title: Measuring Packet Loss and Delay
sections.content:
The OAM toolset MUST measure packet-loss ratio over a pseudowire, LSP, or Section. The ratio is user packets lost divided by user packets sent during a defined interval. Measurement MAY be proactive or on demand, and it SHOULD be possible to use user traffic for the measurement.

The toolset MUST measure one-way delay and, where appropriate, two-way delay. One-way delay runs from transmission of a packet's first bit at one End Point to reception of its last bit at the other End Point. Two-way delay runs from transmission at one End Point until the last bit returns there. A remote data-traffic loopback may measure two-way delay. Accurate one-way measurement may require clock synchronization, which this RFC does not specify.
sections.plainLanguage: OAM must measure packet loss and delay. One-way delay is measured between two endpoints; two-way delay can be measured when a packet returns to its starting endpoint.

sections.title: Congestion and Security
sections.content:
A mechanism such as rate limiting MUST prevent OAM packets from causing congestion in the packet-switched network.

OAM messages can expose sensitive information, including passwords, performance data, and network topology. The RFC suggests authentication, authorization, and encryption, and says management stations SHOULD prevent unauthorized access to OAM functions. Protocol solutions MUST let receivers authenticate message origin and destination, and use of this facility MUST be configurable. An OAM packet received on a pseudowire, LSP, or Section MUST NOT be forwarded beyond that path's End Point.
sections.plainLanguage: OAM must not overload the network. Because OAM messages can reveal sensitive information, systems need configurable authentication and access controls, and must stop OAM packets at the path endpoint.

items.title: Continuity
items.text: Check whether a pseudowire, LSP, or Section is live.

items.title: Connectivity
items.text: Check that the path reaches the expected endpoint.

items.title: Route tracing
items.text: Discover the nodes and interfaces along the path.

items.title: Diagnostics
items.text: Run tests such as loopback or bandwidth estimation.
